sentences.text: This large herbivore measured between 5.5 and 6 meters in length and reached a mass of roughly 2.5 metric tons.
Some estimates suggest the animal could have grown to about 6 meters long and weighed approximately 5 tonnes.
Its scientific name translates to 'face with five horns,' a reference to the three typical horns plus two large epiaugal processes on the cheeks.
The head featured a short nose horn, two long horns on the forehead, and long horns situated on the jugal bones.
The skull possessed a rectangular frill decorated with large triangular osteoderms, including up to twelve episquamosals and three epiparietals.
A distinctive trait of this species is that its very thick jugals do not make contact with the squamosals.
The skull of a specific specimen, cataloged as AMNH 1624, measures an impressive 2.3 meters in length.
Its frill was considerably longer than that of Triceratops and featured two large holes known as parietal fenestrae.
Fossils of this animal were first discovered in 1921.
The initial specimens were collected by Charles Hazelius Sternberg within the San Juan Basin of New Mexico.
Henry Fairfield Osborn formally named and described the species Pentaceratops sternbergii in 1923.
The genus Pentaceratops received its name in 1923 when the type species, Pentaceratops sternbergii, was officially described.
Like all members of the Ceratopsia group, Pentaceratops was an herbivore.
It utilized a sharp beak to bite branches, which were subsequently shredded by its tooth batteries.
Dietary analysis suggests it likely fed on ferns, cycads, and conifers, as flowering plants were geographically limited during its time.
Evidence indicates that Pentaceratops likely exhibited gregarious behavior, similar to most other ceratopsians.
Taxonomically, Pentaceratops is classified within Ceratopsia, specifically belonging to either the Ceratopsinae or Chasmosaurinae subfamilies.
Current classification places the genus firmly within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Phylogenetic studies suggest that Pentaceratops appears to be most closely related to the genus Utahceratops.
The genus Pentaceratops was established by Osborn in 1923.
A new species, Pentaceratops aquilonius, was named by Longrich in 2014.
Pentaceratops lived approximately 76 to 73 million years ago, with most fossils found in the Kirtland Formation of the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
The animal lived approximately 76 to 73 million years ago.
Remains have been mostly found in the Kirtland Formation in the San Juan Basin in New Mexico.
Fossils were also found in the Fruitland Formation dating to the Campanian, approximately 75 million years ago.
Pentaceratops lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
The species was common in the Fruitland and Kirtland formations and serves as a guide fossil marking the transition between the Judith and Kirtland vertebrate eras.
In 2016, researchers suggested that Pentaceratops aquilonius might be the same species as Spiclypeus shipporum and considered it a nomen dubium.
Fowler and Freedman Fowler (2020) debated whether Pentaceratops fenestratus is a distinct taxon from Pentaceratops sternbergii.
It is debated whether the largest specimen should remain in Pentaceratops or be classified as the separate genus Titanoceratops.
Identifying specimens as Pentaceratops has sometimes been highly controversial.
